text.p: Sarajevo's war-weary citizens welcomed Moslem leader Alija Izetbegovic's victory as first chairman of Bosnia's new collective presidency, but said they hoped the days of nationalism were numbered.

"He is the lesser evil among the nationalist leaders and unfortunately at the moment, they are our destiny. I hope he will keep his promise about multi-this and multi-that," Damir, a 23-year-old student, told Reuters.
Izetbegovic narrowly defeated hardline Bosnian Serb rival Momcilo Krajisnik in the race for the three-man presidency which will include the Croat representative Kresimir Zubak.

All three men comfortably beat off challenges for their respective seats, but Izetbegovic polled more votes overall and becomes the body's first chairman. He will hold the rotating post for two years when new elections will be called.

Sarajevo's taxidrivers, traditional SDA voters, immediately paraded through city centre in a long convoy, hooting horns and and waving party flags. They gathered outside the presidency building, chanting pro-Izetbegovic slogans.
The smiling 70-year-old leader, who came to symbolise the Bosnian government's defiance through more than three years of war, appeared briefly and waved at them from a balcony.
Later, he told journalists his political goal was the reintegration of the ethnically-split country with "justice for all".
Elsewhere, with the memories of war still fresh, celebrations were muted.
Several people distinguished between support for Izetbegovic and for his Party of Democratic Action (SDA) and said they hoped he would distance himself from nationalist aides.
"Every normal person voted for Izetbegovic. He's the only one out of the three nationalist leaders who called for a common life and fought for that all the time," said Meliha Isakovic, 39, a dentist.
On the other side of the former front lines, local Serbs said they were resigned to having a Moslem president.
Zoran Stevic, a refugee living in the strategic town of Brcko, said although he would have preferred it if Krajisnik had won, he would accept the result.
"I don't think there will be any problems," he said. "The people have had enough of war... In the end, we will have our own president of the Bosnian Serb Republic, Biljana Plavsic."

Another refugee in Brcko, 19-year-old Natasa who used to live in Sarajevo agreed: "Everything will go back to normal in time, and maybe it won't be important who is (federation) president, because, everyone will have his own (entity) president anyway."
In elections for federal and regional assemblies, the same nationalist parties that led Bosnia to war in 1992 were set to retain power.
"Only Izetbegovic can lead the country in this transition period... just you wait for the next elections, there will be no more nationalist parties here," said Branka, a young unemployed woman.
Critics say both the Moslem leader and his party have become increasingly intolerant and now espouse narrow nationalism.
"Who else could have won? He is the best guarantee Bosnian Moslems will never be slaughtered again," said Hasim Sijercic, a 64-year-old pensioner.

Carl Bildt, the international community's representative in Bosnia, later met Izetbegovic and urged him to lose no time creating common institutions foreseen in the Dayton peace accords to try and reunify the shattered country.
The presidency will meet in Sarajevo, but it is not certain when or where -- a symbolic event likely to involve much negotiation.
